subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: What would happen if a secondary alcohol such as 2-propanol were subjected to mild oxidation?

options.text: It would form an aldehyde that is then rapidly oxidized further to a carboxylic acid
It would form an ether by losing water and joining a second alcohol molecule
It would form a ketone, which resists further oxidation under the same conditions
It would resist oxidation, because its carbinol carbon carries no hydrogen atom

explanation:
Oxidation of an alcohol removes the hydroxyl hydrogen along with a hydrogen from the carbinol carbon. A secondary alcohol has exactly one hydrogen on that carbon, so oxidation stops at the ketone; 2-propanol (C3H8O, about 60 g/mol) becomes acetone (C3H6O, about 58 g/mol), a loss of 60 − 58 = 2 g/mol corresponding to two hydrogen atoms. Primary alcohols keep a second carbinol hydrogen after forming an aldehyde and can therefore proceed to a carboxylic acid, while tertiary alcohols have no carbinol hydrogen at all, which is what choice D actually describes.

ELI-10: Count the hydrogens on the carbon that holds the —OH, because that number sets how far oxidation can go. A primary alcohol's carbinol carbon has two, so it can be oxidized twice, first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol's has one, so oxidation runs once and stops at a ketone. A tertiary alcohol's has none and is essentially inert to this reaction. The mass bookkeeping confirms it: 60 − 58 = 2 g/mol, exactly the two hydrogens removed when 2-propanol becomes acetone.
